podcast.title: Film Appearance - Paradise in Harlem (1938)
podcast.body: Lucky Millinder appeared in the 1938 all-Black film "Paradise in Harlem" with his band, featuring Bill Doggett on piano. "he appeared with Melinda in the 1938 All Black Film Paradise in Harlem, playing on this song."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Band Acquisition Strategy
podcast.body: Lucky Millinder had a unique method of forming his orchestra: he would buy out and assume leadership of existing bands, which would then become the Lucky Millinder Orchestra. "The way Melinda worked was that he bought out and took over the leadership of, existing bands, which then became the Lucky Melinda Orchestra."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Big Band Leader
podcast.body: Millinder was a big band leader who brought Sister Rosetta Tharp into his band after she gained attention at the Cafe Society. "While she was working there, she came to the attention of Lucky Melinda, the big band leader."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Early Collaborations and Hires
podcast.body: Millinder worked with Bill Doggett before Doggett joined The Ink Spots' backing band. For his first hit, Millinder hired trumpet player Dizzy Gillespie, who had recently been fired from Cab Calloway's band after stabbing Calloway in the leg. "He'd worked with Bill Doggett before Doggett went off to join the ink spots backing band, and the trumpet player on his first hit was Dizzy Gillespie, who Melinda had hired after Gillespie had been sacked from CapCalloway's band after stabbing Calloway in the leg."

podcast.title: Female Singers in the 1940s
podcast.body: At the beginning of the 1940s, Rosetta Tharpe was his female singer, providing occasional lead vocals. He also later worked with Ruth Brown. "He had rose at a tharp as his female singer at the beginning of the 40s, and Ruth Brown, who we'll talk about later."

podcast.title: Forgotten Figure in Black Music
podcast.body: Lucky Millinder, though largely overlooked today, was one of the most significant figures in black music during the 1940s, known for his compelling personality and influential role. "Lucky Melinda is a largely forgotten figure now, but he was one of the most important figures in black music in the 1940s."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Leader of Mills Blue Rhythm Band
podcast.body: Millinder started his career as the leader of the Mills Blue Rhythm Band, which served as the house band at the Cotton Club, before moving on to lead his own ensemble. "Later on, he'd started out as the leader of the mill's Blue Rhythm band, the house band in the cotton club."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 7: "Good Rockin' Tonight" by Wynonie Harris

podcast.title: Non-Instrumentalist Leader
podcast.body: Lucky Millinder served as a frontman and occasional singer for his orchestra but could not play any instrument himself. He relied heavily on his musicians, particularly Bill Doggett, to work out arrangements. "Melinda was a frontman and occasional singer, but he couldn't play an instrument, and was reliant on the musicians in his band to work the arrangements out for him."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Non-Musician Talent Recognizer
podcast.body: Millinder did not play instruments, read music, or sing frequently, but he possessed an exceptional ability to identify and cultivate musical talent in others. "What Melinda could definitely do was recognize talent."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Origin of "Lucky" Nickname
podcast.body: A popular story suggests that Al Capone, after losing $10,000 in dice, was offered good luck by Millinder rubbing the dice. Capone subsequently won $50,000 and called him "Lucky" ever since. However, it's more probable that "Lucky" was a shortening of his birth name, Lucius, with the anecdote reflecting the kind of people Millinder associated with. "One story about how he got his name is that Al Capone was down $10,000 playing dice. Melinda offered to rub the dice for luck, and Capone ended the night $50,000 up and called him lucky from then on."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Pioneer of Rhythm and Blues
podcast.body: Millinder's band is widely considered a strong candidate for being the first rhythm and blues band, as they uniquely combined boogie, jump, and jive sounds with a powerful blues feeling, specifically designed to make people dance. "And if you want to point to one band that you can call the first rhythm in Blue's band, you probably want to look at Melinda's band, who more than any other band of the era were able to combine all the boogie, jump, and give sounds with a strong blues feeling and get people dancing."

podcast.title: Replacement of Wynonie Harris (1940s)
podcast.body: After Wynonie Harris left the band to pursue a solo career, Lucky Millinder replaced him with Henry Glover, a trumpet player and singer. "Harris went solo, and Lucky Millinda replaced him with a trumpet player and singer called Henry Glover."

podcast.title: Residency at The Savoy
podcast.body: Millinder's own band secured a main residency at The Savoy, a prominent venue, and also undertook occasional tours on the "Chitlin' Circuit." "Before moving on to lead, asked his own band, one of the main bands in residence at the Savoy, along with occasionally touring the Chitlin circuit."

podcast.title: Savoy Ballroom Residency
podcast.body: After Tharp joined, Millinder's band had a residency at the Savoy Ballroom, becoming very popular with dancers in New York. "Soon after she joined Millen does band, they move to a residency at the Savoy Ballroom, and became one of the most popular bands for dancers in New York."

podcast.title: Savoy Residency Successor
podcast.body: The incarnation of Lucky Millinder's Orchestra, initially formed by Bill Doggett, secured a residency at The Savoy nightclub after Chick Webb's band stopped performing there, under the management of Mo Gale. "This incarnation of the Lucky Melinda Orchestra, the one that was put together by Doggert before Melinda took the band over, is the one that got a residency at the Savoy, after Chick Webb's band stopped playing there."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Talent for Sacking Musicians
podcast.body: Lucky Millinder had a habit of dismissing musicians from his band before they fully realized their potential, as exemplified by his quick sacking of a young Dizzy Gillespie. "Gillespie was quickly sacked by Melinda, who had a habit of getting rid of musicians before they reached their full potential."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Transition to Jump Band Style
podcast.body: Throughout the 1940s, Millinder progressively shifted his band's sound from the popular swing music of the 1930s to the more contemporary jump band style, which was gaining widespread appeal. "Slowly, during the 1940s, Melinda transitioned his band from the kind of swing music that had been popular in the 30s to the jump band style that was becoming more popular."

podcast.title: Unsuccessful Audition by Ray Charles
podcast.body: Ray Charles, after moving to the West Coast, unsuccessfully auditioned to play piano with Lucky Millinder's band. "He moved to the West Coast, and unsuccessfully auditioned to play piano with Lucky Millen does band..."
